docs: stop claiming zero telemetry now that crash reporting ships (#954)

ADR-0020 added Sentry crash reporting (desktop, default ON, opt-out), which reversed a published
"no telemetry" promise. The prose in README.md and SECURITY.md was rewritten at the time, but three
summary claims were missed and kept asserting the old promise:

- README.md Privacy bullet — ~70 lines below the paragraph that correctly names Sentry, in the
  same file, so the README contradicted itself.
- The landing home page's "Privacy-first" card.
- branding/marketing/build.mjs — sub-headline and pill, which pair it with "run 100% offline",
  so the two claims compounded. The rendered 04-private-ai.png is regenerated to match; the other
  three slides re-rendered byte-identical, so no font or renderer drift.

All three now say "no analytics" and name the opt-out crash report, matching the /privacy page and
the "Crash reporting" vocabulary entry in docs/CONTEXT.md.

Left alone deliberately: the two extension-scoped claims. The extension is excluded from Sentry and
declares data_collection_permissions ['none'] to Firefox AMO, so "no telemetry" is true there and
load-bearing for that filed declaration.

Adds check 6 to scripts/check-landing-drift.mjs: a denylist for "zero/no telemetry" over README.md,
SECURITY.md, branding/ and the landing source, scanning by root rather than an explicit file list so
a new marketing surface is covered when it lands. Allowlists the extension privacy section and the
tech-radar entry, whose rationale narrates the reversal rather than claiming it. Verified
non-vacuous: reintroducing the phrase in README.md fails the check.

Corrects two claims in ADR-0020's Consequences section. It said README, SECURITY.md, ARCHITECTURE.md
and CONTEXT.md "were rewritten in the same change" — the rewrite was incomplete. It also credited
check-parity.mjs and check-landing-drift.mjs with failing the build when code and copy disagree;
neither mentioned Sentry or telemetry, and check-parity is a copy-preservation gate that cannot tell
a surviving phrase from a true one. There was no mechanical guard at all, which is why it drifted.

feat: add the cologne navy resume template and a shared navy letter layout (#953)

* feat: add the cologne navy resume template and a shared navy letter layout

Ports the supplied Cologne Navy design into the Typst backend as a 13th
template, plus a fourth cover-letter layout in matching styling.

Three of the brief's assumptions did not hold against this codebase, and each
changed the work:

Carlito is ALREADY bundled, and `FontFamily::Calibri` already resolves to it in
Typst — the metric-compatible substitution the brief asks for is the repo's
existing convention, so the "check whether it's bundled, add it if not" step was
already satisfied.

Letter templates are NOT per resume template. There are three shared layouts
behind a `LetterLayout` enum, chosen independently of the resume template. So
this adds a FOURTH shared layout, offered to every template and inheriting
whichever palette is active — a Regent user selecting Navy gets Regent's
burgundy. Confirmed as the intent before building it.

`base` as a per-template size option conflicts with the model here: `_scale.typ`
is a locked shared house scale and the only per-template knobs that reach a
template are page size, accent, lang, ats and has_photo. The design's
"everything is a multiple of base" property is preserved as ratios off body_pt;
adding a real size option would be a pipeline change across all thirteen
templates, not a template addition.

The reference also consumed its own rich schema (skills groups, project
stack/links, footnotes rows). This repo has ONE generic IR every template
shares, so what is ported is the LOOK, not the schema — the same way meridian
and throughline style identical `sections[].blocks[]` differently. Nothing was
invented and no section dropped.

DEVIATION worth reading: the brief's 0.14em name / 0.18em heading tracking makes
the PDF text extract letter-by-letter — the name came back as
"À LVA R O   È S P O S I T O" and headings as "S U M M A R Y". For a
job-application tool that is an ATS-unreadable name, not a cosmetic issue.
Reduced to 0.06em / 0.10em, the widest values that still extract, and inside the
0.03–0.10em band every other template here already uses. Caught by the
every-template extraction test, which fails at the brief's values.

Also fixes three stale counts found while wiring this up, all unnoticed because
the generators are ignored by CI: the cover-preview generator asserted 10 files
against a 12-entry list (so it could not be run at all), the showcase banner
hardcoded COLS=12 and panicked with an out-of-bounds pixel write on a 13th cell,
and both printed hardcoded counts in their success messages. All now derive from
the canonical list.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: stop the navy letter rendering as banded in docx, and unhardcode its tracking

Five review findings.

The DOCX letter renderer branched on a single `is_refined` boolean, so Navy fell
into the else and inherited BANDED's decoration — the shaded header band and the
short rule footer, neither of which the Navy design has. The same export
therefore produced a Navy PDF and a Banded DOCX. Split out `is_banded` for the
two branches that are genuinely Banded-only, and gave Navy its own centred
letterhead over a bottom rule, which is the parser-safe echo of the .typ. The
branches Navy legitimately shares with Banded (uppercase name, bolded
date/recipient) stay on `!is_refined` rather than being duplicated.

Navy had no DOCX coverage at all. It now joins the three enumerated loops
(font-size ceiling, letterhead-less, subject-line) and the distinct-bytes test,
where the load-bearing pair is Navy vs Banded — that assertion fails against the
old boolean.

`cologne_navy.typ` set fonts as bare strings while every other template, its own
PR sibling included, uses a fallback tuple. Given fallbacks are how the bundled
Carlito is reached in the first place, that was a real gap, not a style nit.

`heading_tracking: 0.18` in the registry was both dead and wrong — the template
hardcoded 0.10em. The template now reads the field and the registry says 0.10,
so the source of truth is single and the extraction constraint is recorded where
someone changing it will look.

And the tier-badge test asserted only an aggregate count, which would still pass
if a different card supplied the eighth ATS badge and cologne-navy were missing
entirely. Added an assertion naming the card.

* fix: route every navy docx branch by feature, not by "not refined"

The review was right that my first pass was partial, and finishing it found two
more mismatches it had not named.

I split only the header band and the footer rule and left the rest binary, so
Navy still lost Refined's role line and subject caption and still inherited
Banded's bolding. My own commit message claimed Navy "legitimately shares the
bolded date/recipient" with Banded — that was wrong, and checking
letter_navy.typ would have shown it: its emit-date-block and
emit-recipient-block carry no `weight: "bold"`, unlike letter_banded.typ's. I

Replaced the boolean with per-FEATURE flags derived from what each `.typ`

default.

Two further mismatches found while auditing the remaining branches:

The contact line was right-aligned unconditionally, so Navy's centred letterhead
was centred name over a right-aligned contact.

And the letterhead rule sat on the NAME paragraph, drawing a line between the
name and its own contact line. letter_navy.typ rules under the whole block
(name → title → contact), so it belongs on the contact paragraph.

The new test asserts the FEATURES rather than "differs from Banded" — no shaded

* refactor: make each letter layout state its docx style instead of inheriting

Third review round on this function, so patching a fourth branch was the wrong
answer.

The finding was real: the no-profile FALLBACK contact path still right-aligned
Navy with no rule, while the profile-backed path centred it and ruled it. The
same letter rendered differently depending on whether a ContactProfile happened
to be attached.

The cause is structural, not a missed line. A single `is_refined` boolean with
everything else falling through to Banded meant adding a layout inherited
Banded's look by DEFAULT, and each review round found a different survivor:
round one the header band and footer rule, round two the title, subject caption
and bolding, round three this contact path.

Replaced it with a `LetterDocxStyle` filled in per layout — uppercase name, name
size bonus, header band, centred letterhead, title, subject caption, addressing
bold, header rule, footer rule, signature gap, and the two spacing values. Every
call site reads a field, and both contact paths call one `contact_align()` so
they cannot drift apart again. A new layout now fails to compile until someone
states what it does.

The test was weak in the same way the code was: `contains("center")` passed
while the fallback contact was still right-aligned, because centring the NAME
alone satisfied it. It now counts centred and right-aligned paragraphs and
requires at least two centred — verified to fail against the pre-fix fallback.

Behaviour for Classic, Refined and Banded is unchanged; their table entries were
read off the existing branches.

* fix: style navy's docx title and caption from its own typ, not refined's

Both findings are the same defect as the last three rounds, one level down: the
style struct made each feature's PRESENCE layout-aware and left its STYLING
hardcoded to Refined's.

So Navy rendered the role line accent-coloured, uppercased and letter-spaced
while letter_navy.typ puts it in the muted date colour, plain case, untracked;
and the subject caption in the accent colour where the typ uses the name colour.
Presence and style are separate decisions, and asserting only presence missed
both — my previous test checked that Navy SHOWS a title, never how.

Added title_emphasised and caption_uses_name_colour to LetterDocxStyle, both
read off each typ, so the styling now travels with the layout the same way the
feature list does.

The new test asserts the styling rather than the presence: Refined uppercases
and tracks the role line, Navy does neither. Verified to fail against the
hardcoded version.

fix: stop squashing the embeddings checkbox, and unnest the provider row button (#952)

* fix: stop squashing the embeddings checkbox, and unnest the provider row button

Both reported off a screenshot of the shipped UI, plus one found by the log
bridge. All three are things no test covered because nobody had looked.

The two embeddings toggles looked like different controls. One cause: the row is
`justify-between` with no gap and the `<input>` had no `shrink-0`. Semantic
scoring's one-line description leaves slack so it renders correctly; the longer
auto-index description fills the row, so the copy butts against the checkbox AND
flexbox compresses the input below its own h-4 w-4. Not a different checkbox —
a squashed one. Fixed on both rows so a future copy change to either cannot
bring it back.

`ProviderRow` wrapped its header in a `<Button>` and nested the "test key"
`<Button>` inside it: invalid DOM, and clicking test-key also toggled the row's
expand. React had been reporting it as "<button> cannot contain a nested
<button>" into devtools where nobody saw it; it only became visible once the
renderer console bridge started writing to the log file. Converted to the
repo's existing `role="button"` row pattern (see NotificationBell), which keeps
Enter/Space activation without the nesting.

Writing the tests surfaced a third: the semantic-scoring checkbox had no
aria-label. Added.

Asserted on classes rather than geometry — jsdom reports zero width/height, so a
computed-size assertion would have passed against the broken markup. Both layout
tests were verified to fail against the shipped version.

* fix: stop the test-key click from also expanding the provider row

Flagged by both the pre-push gate and the CI review, and they were right about

matches the role="button" row too, so it flagged the legitimate real-button-
inside-role-button-row pattern. It now checks actual <button> elements, which
is what React's rule is about.

feat: index documents automatically, and stop the index strip reading as a chore (#951)

* feat: index documents automatically, and stop the index strip reading as a chore

Reported as "I have to go to AI settings and press the indexing button after
uploading a résumé". Tracing it first: that was never true. `match_resume`
already embeds lazily when it finds no usable vector and caches the result, so
the Settings button is a pre-warm, not a prerequisite. What it actually cost was
a slow first match and a status strip that looked like a task list.

Three parts.

**Say what is true.** The strip said "N documents need re-indexing for the active
model" in amber. Nothing needs it — matching indexes on first use. Reworded, and
no longer styled as a warning, with a separate line for when auto-indexing is on.

**Auto-index, opt in.** New `autoIndexOnUpload` preference. One hook mounted at
the root covers all three moments that create stale documents, because they all
surface identically as a non-zero `documents.stale`: a fresh import, an embedding
provider/model change, and leftovers from a previous session.

Backed by a NEW command rather than the existing one: `ai_reembed_all` re-embeds
every document unconditionally, so reusing it would re-bill a cloud embedding
provider for already-indexed documents each time a single file is added.
`ai_index_stale_documents` embeds only what is missing and returns a null job id
when nothing is. Both share one job body so they cannot drift in error handling,
cancellation or progress.

**Ask during setup.** New onboarding step immediately before the crash-reporting
consent — both ask "may this run on your behalf", and this one calls a provider
that may bill per token, so the two spend/privacy decisions sit together.

Defaults to OFF, and the step's switch is seeded from the stored value rather
than forced on: an existing install must never start calling a paid embedding
provider because of an update, and stepping back through the wizard must not
silently discard a "no". Leaving it off costs nothing — matching still indexes
lazily, which is the whole point of the first part.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: auto-index a second upload that leaves the same stale count

The AI review found a HIGH in the guard I wrote, and it was right: the dedup key
was `provider/model/staleCount` and never reset. Import one résumé (stale 1,
indexed), import another (stale 1 again) and the second matched the previous key
and was skipped — auto-indexing silently died after the very first document. A
count identifies a situation, not a batch.

Two things were needed, and each protects against the other's failure mode.

Hold the concurrency guard until the JOB ends, not until indexStaleDocuments
resolves. That returns as soon as the job is spawned, so the status refetch
straight after it still reports the pre-run count and would start a second,
separately-billed run over the same documents. Now released on the job's
terminal event, via the same useJobEvents path the manual re-index already uses.

Keep a per-(space, count) attempt key, but CLEAR it once the index goes clean or
the space changes. Without the key, a run that fails to reduce the count
re-triggers the instant it ends — an unbounded loop of paid provider calls.
Without the reset, the reported bug.

The guard also had to become state rather than a ref: the effect must re-run
when a job finishes, and clearing a ref re-renders nothing.

Both halves are pinned, and the regression test was verified to fail against the
original guard rather than assumed to: removing the reset reproduces exactly the
reported symptom.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: never run two embedding jobs at once, and stop the strip guessing

Three review findings.

Auto-indexing and the manual "Re-index now" button were independent triggers
with no knowledge of each other, so a background auto-index and a button press
could embed the same documents concurrently — billing a cloud provider twice for
identical work. Guarded in the BACKEND rather than by disabling the button:
that is the one place every trigger has to pass through, and a UI-only guard
narrows the race instead of closing it. A second trigger now returns the running
job id, so the caller watches that run instead of starting a duplicate. No new
state — JobTracker already records kind and status.

The strip inferred "indexing them now" from the auto-index PREFERENCE alone,
so it claimed work was happening even when the run had already failed, or was
never started because nothing had changed. `ai_embedding_status` now reports
whether an embedding job is actually running and the strip reads that.

And the step's top doc comment still said the switch "defaults ON" while the
code — and a comment twelve lines below it — did the opposite. Left over from
the first draft; the opt-in behaviour is the correct one, so the comment was
what needed fixing.

The guard's per-record decision is split out as a pure predicate so it can be
tested without the AppHandle this crate has no harness for. The load-bearing
case is the differential: a COMPLETED job must not count as active, or the guard
latches after the first run and auto-indexing never fires again.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: make the embed-job claim atomic and the completion listener race-proof

Two review findings, and closing the second surfaced a harder race than the one
reported.

The guard was check-then-act: `running_embed_job` then `job_start` are two
separate lock acquisitions, so two commands can both observe "nothing running"
before either registers. Scan and insert now share one lock via
`JobTracker::start_exclusive`.

That returns `Option`, not `Result`. R6 caught the first attempt for banning
`Result<_, String>`, and the rule was pointing at a real modelling error: "a job
is already running" is not a failure, it is the job the caller should watch. The
type says that now.

The completion listener compared against the `inFlightJob` STATE.
`setInFlightJob` only schedules a render, so a job finishing before that render
commits hits a closure still holding `null`, drops its own completion, and
latches the guard forever — auto-indexing dead until restart. Now compared
against a ref written synchronously alongside the state, the same fix
`EmbeddingsSettings` already documents for `reindexJobIdRef`.

Writing the regression test for that exposed a second ordering: a job can finish
before the invoke that created it even RESOLVES (an index where every document
fails returns almost immediately), so the completion arrives before there is any
claim to match. The ref alone does not help there. Terminal ids seen without a
claim are now remembered briefly, and a claim for one of them releases
immediately instead of waiting for an event that already passed.

Both races are pinned, and both tests were verified to fail against the previous
code rather than assumed to.

fix: map local Ollama's stop reason, and stop presuming an OpenAI embedding model (#950)

* fix: map local ollama's stop reason and stop presuming an openai embedding model

Two follow-ups from #948, both verified against the code first.

**Local Ollama never reported a stop reason.** `parse_ollama_frames` set `usage`
on the final sentinel but skipped `done_reason`, which rides on that same object
— so `stream::finish` could not tell "the model burned its whole output budget
reasoning and never answered" from "the provider silently returned nothing" for
local Ollama. That is the exact ambiguity that made an empty generation
unexplainable in the macOS report.

The non-streaming agent path (`parse_ollama_turn`) already read the field, so the
mapping is extracted to `ollama_done_reason` and shared rather than copied — a
second hand-written copy is the duplicated-heuristic defect this codebase keeps
re-learning. Callers keep their own precedence on top (a turn still lets Length
outrank a tool call).

**`text-embedding-3-small` was offered as the default for providers that have
never heard of it.** It is an OpenAI model id, and every OpenAI-compatible client
is built on `OpenAiClient`: Ollama Cloud delegates `default_embedding_model`
straight through, and `OpenAiCompatible` covers LM Studio, vLLM and OpenRouter.
Embedding with any of those and no explicit model posted an OpenAI model to a
gateway that does not host it, and the model-not-found came back reading as
"embeddings are broken" rather than "choose an embedding model".

Gated on `id == OpenAi`, the same way `supports_web_search` already is.

Deliberately NOT flipping `supports_embeddings` to false for those providers,
despite that being how I had recorded this: the boolean is provider-level (the
error text says so, and Anthropic is the only false), the `/v1/embeddings`
endpoint may genuinely exist on a given gateway, and an explicit model the user
knows works must still go through. A per-model allowlist would also break the
zero-code-change rule for new models and risk false negatives that block working
setups. Only the presumed DEFAULT was ever wrong.

Also split the two embedding errors that were identical strings: "no default
model for X, choose one" is fixable by picking a model; "X does not support
embeddings" is not.

fix: make clicking an OS notification open the app, on the right screen (#949)

* fix: make clicking an os notification open the app, on the right screen

Reported twice: clicking a Windows notification does nothing, and there was no
way to jump from a notification to the thing it was about.

Both had one cause. `tauri-plugin-notification`'s desktop `show()` is
notify-rust fire-and-forget, and the `onAction` JS helper its docs point at for
clicks resolves to `plugin:notification|register_listener` — a command the
plugin registers ONLY on mobile (its desktop invoke_handler is exactly notify,
request_permission, is_permission_granted). So the renderer's subscription
failed with "Command not found" on every desktop startup and no banner click
ever reached the app. `notifications_clicked` — which already does the right
thing — had no caller other than the tray.

Show the banner natively instead, per platform, since only Windows is
callback-based:

- Windows: tauri-winrt-notification's on_activated, non-blocking.
- macOS/Linux: notify-rust's wait_for_action BLOCKS, so it runs on
  spawn_blocking. Linux additionally needs a declared `default` action for a
  body click to be delivered at all.

Both crates were already in the tree transitively; they are pinned to the
locked versions so there is no duplicate copy.

Routing: the click now carries the clicked notification's OWN route, so
"Autopilot X found 3 jobs" opens THAT autopilot rather than a list to search.
Every notification source already attached a route (autopilot -> /autopilot with
its id) and the bell already followed it — only the OS banner didn't. Validated
through the same resolveNotificationRoute the bell uses, so an unknown backend
route falls back instead of breaking navigation. A tray click sends no route and
still just opens the inbox.

The dead renderer seam (onOsBannerClick) is removed, which also silences the
startup console error it produced.

Known limit, all platforms: the callback lives in this process, so it fires only
while the app runs. A click after the app exits needs a COM activator on Windows
and is out of scope.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: bound banner listeners and close the windows ci gap

Four review findings, all real.

The macOS/Linux path parks a blocking thread in wait_for_action until the user
clicks or the banner closes — and a notification nobody touches (sitting in
macOS Notification Center) parks it indefinitely. OsBanner::Always sources like
autopilot can emit a burst, so a run of ignored notifications would hold
blocking workers permanently and starve every other spawn_blocking caller.

Bounded to 8 concurrent listeners via an RAII slot (released on Drop, so a panic
inside the wait cannot leak the budget). Over budget the banner is still
DELIVERED — on Linux show() already sent it, and macOS's handle Drop sends it —
it just has no click handler. Losing one banner's click beats starving the pool.
The async alternative was checked and rejected: wait_for_action_async exists
only on Linux, and behind a feature that swaps the dbus backend.

Windows had the same CI hole this branch opened the macOS job for: no PR job
compiles cfg(windows), so the notification code that actually fixes the reported
bug was built only on the dev machine. Added the counterpart.

Also corrected the macOS job's own comment, which overstated the gap:
cfg(not(windows)) IS compiled by the ubuntu jobs — only platform-exclusive
predicates were uncovered.

And the route tests now use the shared NotificationOpen type instead of local
structural aliases; they exist to guard that contract, so a local shape could
not detect drift in it.

fix: the macOS bug report — docx sizes, blocked pdf downloads, empty generations, and logs you can actually read (#948)

* fix: write docx font sizes in half-points, not twentieths of a point

A user's exported CV came out as 132 pages of enormous text. `w:sz` is in
half-points, but every font size went through `pt_to_dxa` (pt × 20 — the
correct unit for spacing, indentation and page geometry, not type). A 10.5pt
body font was written as `w:sz val="210"`, i.e. 105pt. Every DOCX export, on
every platform, since the renderer was written.

24 call sites now route through `pt_to_half_points` (pt × 2, rounded — odd
half-point sizes like 10.5 → 21 are representable and were previously
truncated). The genuine dxa uses — line spacing, section spacing, indents —
are unchanged, and border widths never went through the helper at all.

No test asserted `w:sz` anywhere, which is how a 10× error survived: the
DOCX suite covered page size, fonts and colours only. There are now exact
size assertions for both writers plus a ceiling guard that fails if any run
exceeds 50pt, which catches this whole class rather than these constants.

* fix: key cached match scores on the embedding vector version

Cached semantic scores are computed from embeddings, but the cache key
carried provider, model and formula version — not the vector format. A
format change therefore left every stored score a valid hit against vectors
that no longer mean the same thing.

It has been harmless only by coincidence: the format bump in #933 happened to
land with a MATCH_FORMULA_VERSION bump, and that field IS in the key, so the
scores were invalidated by the formula axis rather than by anything reasoning
about vectors. The next format bump without a coincidental formula bump would
have served stale scores as fresh, silently.

The version is now part of the key and of the table's primary key, so a
format change invalidates by construction. Adding an eviction to each future
migration would have been the patch-the-instance answer, and it depends on
whoever writes the next migration remembering — which is the failure this
already survived once by luck.

Every construction site is exhaustive over the struct, so a new one cannot
omit it.

Found alongside: `posting_vectors` has no persisted version column at all and
synthesizes the current one on read, so it cannot self-detect staleness and
still depends on a hand-written eviction per bump. Left alone — that is a
schema change, not this fix.

* fix: keep a stored cookie's domain scope when rebuilding the jar

Cookies were rebuilt for the reqwest jar as `name=value; Path=...` with no
`Domain`, then added against a URL built from the stored domain with its
leading dot stripped. Per RFC 6265 a cookie with no `Domain` attribute is
host-only, so the leading dot — the very thing marking it as applying to
subdomains — was discarded, and a session captured for `.linkedin.com`
stopped reaching `www.linkedin.com`.

The user-visible effect was that whether a request was authenticated depended
on how the URL happened to be spelled, since both forms pass `detect_platform`.

A stored domain carrying the leading dot now rebuilds with `Domain`, and one
without it stays host-only, matching how it was captured.

Deliberately narrow: `Domain` is only ever the cookie's own stored host, never
anything wider. Widening a session cookie's scope would send a credential to a
host it was never issued for, which is worse than the bug being fixed — so
where the stored shape is ambiguous it stays host-only. `Secure` and
`HttpOnly` were already preserved.

The jar-building loop is extracted so it can be asserted against directly,
`reqwest::Client` not exposing its jar after build. The test that matters is
the safety one — a cookie is never attached to an unrelated host — and it was
confirmed load-bearing by temporarily broadening the code and watching it fail.

docs: consolidate 13 agent rule files into a canonical agents.md (#903)

* docs: consolidate 13 agent rule files into a canonical agents.md

The repo maintained 13 hand-written copies of the same coding rules: CLAUDE.md,
AGENTS.md, .clinerules, .windsurfrules, .codexrules, .roorules, .jba/guidelines.md,
.aider/system-prompt.md, .github/copilot-instructions.md and 4x .cursor/rules/*.mdc.

They had already drifted. `NumberField` — a primitive named in enforced rule 5 — and
the whole apps/landing workspace existed in CLAUDE.md alone, so twelve files taught a
stale rule set. Every rule change meant 13 edits with nothing enforcing the 13th.

AGENTS.md is now canonical: a Linux Foundation standard, read natively by Copilot,
Cursor, Windsurf and Codex. CLAUDE.md imports it with the documented `@AGENTS.md`
syntax and keeps only Claude-Code-specific orchestration — the subagent fleet, review
gates and model tiering, none of which other tools can act on. Files for tools that
don't read AGENTS.md natively or in full become one-line pointers; redundant ones go.

Applied the /doctor trim heuristic while merging: cut what an agent can derive from the
codebase (package layout block, name-to-path lookup rows), kept every enforced rule
verbatim plus the non-obvious locations. All 16 rules survive; the combined load is 136
lines, inside the documented 200-line target.

check-agent-system now enforces the invariant instead of relying on discipline: tool
files must name AGENTS.md and stay under 1KB, so a forked ruleset fails pre-push and
CI. Also fixes .aider.conf.yml, which pointed at a contracts.ts removed long ago.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: correct a nonexistent ui primitive in the canonical rules

Review found rule 5 lists `SelectDropdown` among the required @ajh/ui
primitives. It is not exported — packages/ui/src/index.ts:37 exports
`Dropdown`, and the renderer imports `Dropdown` everywhere. An agent
following the rule writes an import that fails the build.

This was pre-existing drift carried over verbatim, but "all 16 rules
survive verbatim" is the right invariant for the merge and the wrong one
for correctness: verbatim preserved the bug, and the merge just blessed
it as canonical for every tool. Same failure mode as the `NumberField`
staleness this PR exists to fix. Also fixes the ESLint message that fires
on raw <select> and the Form JSDoc, both naming the same missing export.

Enforce the two facts the whole rule set hangs on, which nothing asserted:
AGENTS.md exists, and CLAUDE.md contains an unfenced `@AGENTS.md` import.
Without either, Claude Code loads orchestration with zero coding rules
while every pointer still truthfully says "read AGENTS.md" and the check
stays green. Verified both assertions fail when violated, plus the size
cap on a re-forked pointer.

Exempt .aider.conf.yml from the pointer size cap — it is a real settings
file, so growing past 1KB is legitimate and the message would mislead.

Other review fixes: qualify Copilot's native AGENTS.md support (not all
features, per GitHub docs), rule 13 used grep against the repo's own rg
policy, rule 14 named a contracts.ts removed long ago, and the header
docblock plus a comment still said nine copies and CLAUDE.md.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: close a fenced-import hole in the canonical rules guard

The import guard added last round claimed to catch a "missing or fenced"
import but only caught inline backticks. Under /m, `^` matches at the start
of a line inside a fenced block too, so a triple-backticked @AGENTS.md
passed green while Claude Code skipped the import — the docs are explicit
that import parsing skips code spans and fenced blocks. That is precisely
the failure the guard exists to prevent: orchestration loads, zero coding
rules load, every pointer still truthfully says "read AGENTS.md".

My "verified by fault injection" claim last round covered only the inline
variant. Fences are now stripped before testing, and all three variants are
verified failing: block-fenced, tilde-fenced, and inline backticks.

Cap the canonical files at 200 combined lines. They load in full every
session and adherence drops as they grow; the PR asserted that budget and
then hand-checked it, the same gap as the unenforced import. Now enforced,
with .claude/rules/ + paths: frontmatter named as the escape hatch.

Also: rule 5's `SelectDropdown` rename left one entry behind in
DEEP_UI_IMPORTS, banning a path that no longer exists. The .gitignore
inventory omitted .codexrules and .roorules and claimed the 1KB cap covers
.aider.conf.yml, now exempt. AGENTS.md told non-Claude tools to use an
ownership table that every pointer file tells them to ignore — it now
describes the routing inline.

Verified against vendor docs rather than the secondary sources the deletions
originally rested on: Windsurf processes AGENTS.md through the same rules
engine, and Cursor documents it as a first-class alternative to
.cursor/rules. Both deletions stand.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: correct two dead paths in rule 14 and harden the fence stripper

Rule 14 named `commands.rs` and `services/query-client.ts`; both are
directories on disk (commands/, services/query-client/). Last round fixed
`contracts.ts` on the same line and left its two siblings — the canonical
file for every tool was naming files that are not there.

Harden the fence stripper: matching the full opening run means a 3-backtick
inner fence can no longer close a 4-backtick outer one, and 1-3 leading
spaces are still a fence per CommonMark. Both variants verified failing,
alongside the plain and inline cases.

Restore the Copilot caveat in the .gitignore inventory — that comment is
where someone decides whether a pointer is still needed, and it claimed
unqualified native support that AGENTS.md and the pointer both qualify.

Considered and rejected: a mechanical dead-path check over backticked paths
in the canonical files. First run produced two false positives — `machines/`
(real, under a lookup root I had not listed) and the commit-type list
`refactor/ui/style/...`, which is not a path at all. Catching the shorthand
form that actually broke three times (`commands.rs`, not
`src-tauri/src/commands/`) needs a resolution table that is itself
drift-prone, so the checker would need more maintenance than the rules it
guards.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: guard fully-qualified paths in the canonical rules

Round 3 rejected a dead-path check because the unscoped version produced
false positives. That reasoning conflated two halves. Fully-qualified paths
resolve from the repo root with no lookup table, so nothing drifts;
shorthand needs a workspace-root table that rots like the rules it guards.
Only the first half is checked now, scoped to AGENTS.md.

Verified rather than assumed: 35 backticked slash-tokens in AGENTS.md, 14
qualified, 14/14 resolve, zero false positives. The commitlint type list
that broke the unscoped version is correctly skipped, as is every shorthand
form. Injecting a dead qualified path fails the check; injecting a dead
shorthand path passes, confirming the documented gap is real and not a
guess.

The .gitignore inventory said pointers are kept "only for tools that don't
read it natively / in full", then listed Codex as a native reader and kept
.codexrules — whose own stated reason (an unmissable pointer) the criterion
did not admit. Widened the criterion instead of dropping the file.

* feat: revoke extension pairing over the bridge on token rotation

Rotating the pairing token (Settings -> Regenerate, or a factory reset) left
live authenticated sockets running and the connected count up, and a
reconnecting extension only saw the deliberately silent failed-handshake close
- indistinguishable from a crashed app - so it retried the dead token forever
and never returned to its pairing view.

Adds a desktop -> extension `token.revoked` frame (TS constants + zod enum and
the Rust msg mirror, in lockstep). BridgeState::regenerate_token now signals
every live connection task, zeroes the live-connection count, then swaps the
secret, all inside the token lock so no handshake can authenticate against the
old token and miss the revoke. Only an ALREADY-AUTHENTICATED socket is sent the
frame; an unauthenticated one closes silently as before, preserving the
no-token-oracle invariant (ADR-0010). The frame carries no payload and no token
material.

The extension drops its stored token through the same local un-pair path the
popup's Unpair button uses, skips the backoff loop, and re-probes once unpaired
so the popup lands on the pairing view. Old extensions ignore an unknown wire
type, so no protocol-version bump is needed.

Also moves the msg constant table into its own module (the addition pushed
extension_bridge/mod.rs past the R8 hard LOC cap) and mentions re-pairing in the
factory-reset confirm copy (en + de).

* fix: honor token.revoked only on an authenticated bridge session

The `handshakeFrame` intercept is a step-in-flight latch, not an auth check:
`awaitHandshakeFrame`'s `settle` nulls it the instant a step's frame is
consumed, so a frame arriving between steps - notably while `computeProof` is
awaited - fell through to the type dispatch. A port-squatter needs zero token
knowledge to send a syntactically-valid `challenge`, then a `token.revoked`, to
destroy the stored pairing credential; the revoke close path's backoff reset
made that loopable. The pre-hello window and the no-token attach (which reaches
phase `connected` with no handshake at all) were exposed the same way.

Adds a real `authenticated` flag on BridgeClient, set only where serverProof
verification completes and cleared on every attach and on close, and gates the
revoke branch on it. The branch stays below the handshake intercept so both
protections compose.

Tests: the security probe is now permanent (valid-challenge-then-revoke during
the computeProof window must not unpair), plus a stale-frame-after-close probe
and a revoke aimed at the unpaired re-probe socket - both verified to fail
without their respective guard.

Also: a failed token clear now forces bad_token instead of silently retrying a
known-dead secret, and the rotation lock-scope comments no longer overclaim
(the proof is verified outside the token lock; safety rests on
subscribe-at-accept plus the buffered broadcast).

* fix: bind the bridge handshake verdict to the transport that earned it

WS5 defense-in-depth. `authenticated` is set after `await computeProof(...)`,
so a socket that closes inside that await had the flag cleared by `onClose` and
then set straight back by the resuming continuation - leaving it true with a
null transport until the next attach, and `setPhase('connected')` claiming a
live session over nothing. Only a valid serverProof reaches that line, so it
was not peer-reachable, but a stale-true auth flag on the bridge is worth zero
tolerance: the next frame delivered on that dead transport would be trusted.

Re-checks the captured transport identity before applying the verdict. Plain
return rather than finishHandshake: whatever ended the transport already set
its phase and armed its reconnect, and finishHandshake would null and close
`this.transport` - which in the replaced case is a different, healthy socket.

Test: socket closes during the serverProof await -> phase never becomes
connected and a following token.revoked is ignored. Verified to fail before the
guard (phase came back connected on a dead transport).
